introduction-when-fast-enough-isnt.core: At 10–100 Gbps a server has only nanoseconds per packet: 64-byte packets at 10 Gbps arrive every 67 ns, about 200 CPU cycles. The default kernel path (interrupt, buffer allocation, protocol stack, copy to user space) can't keep up per core. High-performance networking pushes work to hardware (offloads), batches it (coalescing, GRO), spreads it across cores (RSS), bypasses layers (SR-IOV, DPDK, XDP) and enlarges units (jumbo frames).

first_principles.problem: A 25 Gbps NIC delivers only 6 Gbps because one CPU core is pegged at 100% handling interrupts.
truths: Per-packet costs dominate at high rates.

analogy.title: A post office at Christmas
analogy.story: Clerks can't hand-sort every letter, so you add machines (offload), bundle mail (batching), open more counters (RSS), and use express lanes (bypass).
analogy.breaks: Post offices hire seasonal staff; servers have fixed cores.

code.text:
mpstat -P ALL 1 | head -20          # one core at 100% softirq?
cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0    # all IRQs on CPU0?
ethtool -S eth0 | grep -E 'drop|miss'

check.q: Roughly how often do 64-byte packets arrive at 10 Gbps line rate?
check.a: About every 67 ns (~14.88 million packets per second).

interrupt-coalescing-batching-the-doorbe.core: Raising a CPU interrupt for every packet costs thousands of cycles in context switching. Interrupt coalescing makes the NIC wait for N packets or T microseconds before interrupting, and Linux NAPI switches to polling under load, processing a batch per interrupt. The trade-off is latency against throughput: more coalescing means fewer interrupts and higher throughput but adds microseconds of delay. Adaptive coalescing tunes it automatically.

first_principles.problem: A trading system needs microsecond latency, but default coalescing adds 50 µs per packet.

analogy.title: A doorbell for every parcel vs a delivery schedule
analogy.story: Answering the door for each parcel wastes time; batched deliveries save effort but you wait a bit longer.
analogy.breaks: Couriers don't adapt; adaptive coalescing does.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Latency vs throughput tuned per workload.

code.text:
ethtool -c eth0                        # current settings
ethtool -C eth0 adaptive-rx on         # general purpose
ethtool -C eth0 adaptive-rx off rx-usecs 0 rx-frames 1   # lowest latency
sysctl -w net.core.busy_poll=50        # busy-poll sockets

check.q: What's the main downside of aggressive interrupt coalescing?
check.a: Added latency, since packets wait in the NIC until the batch threshold or timer fires.

receive-side-scaling-rss-spreading-the-l.core: Modern NICs have many receive queues. RSS hashes each packet's flow (IPs and ports) to pick a queue, and each queue's interrupt is bound to a different CPU core, so flows are processed in parallel while each flow stays ordered on one core. RPS and RFS do the same in software for NICs without RSS, and steer packets to the core where the consuming application runs.

first_principles.problem: A 16-core load balancer uses only one core for networking because RSS is disabled.
truths: Hashing keeps a flow on one queue.
derivation: Set **IRQ affinity** per queue to cores.
Mind **NUMA**: queues near the NIC's node.

analogy.title: Multiple checkout lanes by surname
analogy.story: Customers are assigned a lane by surname so families stay together, and all cashiers work in parallel.
analogy.breaks: Customers choose lanes; one elephant flow can still overload one core.

code.text:
ethtool -l eth0                 # max combined queues
ethtool -L eth0 combined 16
ethtool -x eth0                 # indirection table
for q in /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-*; do echo ffff > $q/rps_cpus; done

check.q: Why does RSS hash by flow rather than spreading packets randomly?
check.a: To keep packets of the same flow on one queue/core and preserve ordering.

tcp-offloading-making-hardware-do-the-wo.core: NICs can take over repetitive TCP/IP work. Checksum offload computes checksums in hardware. TSO (TCP Segmentation Offload) lets the kernel hand the NIC one 64 KB buffer, which it cuts into MSS-sized packets; LRO/GRO merge received packets into large buffers before the stack sees them. That cuts per-packet CPU dramatically, but captures look odd (huge packets) and LRO can break routing or forwarding, so GRO is preferred.

first_principles.problem: CPU usage hits 80% at 10 Gbps transfers because segmentation offloads were disabled during debugging and never re-enabled.
truths: Fewer, bigger units mean less overhead.

analogy.title: Sending one big box and letting the depot split it
analogy.story: Instead of packing 40 small boxes yourself, hand one big box to the depot that splits and labels them.
analogy.breaks: Depots don't confuse inspectors; offloads confuse packet captures.

code.text:
ethtool -k eth0 | grep -E 'segmentation|receive-offload|checksum'
# tcp-segmentation-offload: on
# generic-receive-offload: on
# large-receive-offload: off
ethtool -K eth0 tso on gro on

check.q: Why might tcpdump show 64 KB TCP packets on a 1500-MTU link?
check.a: Capture happens before TSO segmentation (or after GRO merging), so you see the large buffers the kernel handles.

jumbo-frames-bigger-boxes-less-tape.core: The standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes. Jumbo frames (typically 9000) carry six times more payload per packet, so there are fewer packets, fewer interrupts and less header overhead for bulk transfers such as storage, replication and backups. Every device on the path (NICs, switches, routers, hypervisors) must support the same MTU, or large packets get dropped or fragmented, and internet paths stay at 1500.

first_principles.problem: Enabling MTU 9000 on servers breaks NFS because one switch in the path still has MTU 1500.
truths: One small-MTU hop breaks large packets.

analogy.title: Shipping in larger crates
analogy.story: Fewer crates mean less handling, but every door along the route must be wide enough.
analogy.breaks: Crates that don't fit are noticed; jumbo frames are silently dropped.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Confirms jumbo path before relying on it.

code.text:
ip link set eth1 mtu 9000
ping -M do -s 8972 -c 3 10.50.0.20     # 8972 + 28 = 9000
# 'message too long' or loss → a hop has smaller MTU

check.q: Why is 8972 used as the ping payload to test a 9000 MTU?
check.a: IPv4 header (20) + ICMP header (8) = 28 bytes, so 8972 + 28 = 9000.

sr-iov-high-performance-for-virtual-mach.core: Virtualised networking normally passes every packet through a software switch in the hypervisor, adding CPU cost and latency. SR-IOV lets one physical NIC present many virtual functions (VFs) that are assigned directly to VMs or pods, so the guest driver talks to hardware and bypasses the hypervisor's data path. That gives near-native throughput and latency. The costs are lost live migration (in many setups), limited VFs, and less software-level visibility and filtering.

first_principles.problem: A virtualised network function can't exceed 5 Gbps through the hypervisor's virtual switch.
truths: NICs can expose multiple PCIe functions.

analogy.title: Giving tenants their own direct phone lines
analogy.story: Instead of all calls going through the building switchboard, each tenant gets a line straight to the exchange.
analogy.breaks: Direct lines are easy to move; VFs often block live migration.

code.text:
echo 8 > /sys/class/net/ens1f0/device/sriov_numvfs
ip link show ens1f0       # vf 0..7 listed
ip link set ens1f0 vf 0 vlan 100 spoofchk on mac 52:54:00:12:34:56

check.q: Why does SR-IOV often prevent live migration?
check.a: The VM is tied to a physical VF on a specific NIC, whose hardware state can't be easily moved to another host.

kernel-bypass-and-dpdk-skipping-the-midd.core: DPDK moves packet processing entirely into user space. Poll-mode drivers own the NIC (unbinding it from the kernel), huge pages hold pre-allocated packet buffers, and dedicated cores spin polling the receive rings, avoiding interrupts, syscalls and copies. It reaches tens of millions of packets per second per core, at the cost of burning cores at 100%, losing the kernel's TCP/IP stack and tools, and much greater complexity.

first_principles.problem: A software firewall needs to process 40 Mpps, which the kernel stack can't reach.

analogy.title: A private express lane with dedicated staff
analogy.story: Packages skip the main sorting hall entirely, handled by staff who do nothing but watch the conveyor.
analogy.breaks: Staff can rest; polling cores are 100% busy even when idle.

code.text:
echo 2048 > /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages
dpdk-devbind.py --bind=vfio-pci 0000:3b:00.0
dpdk-testpmd -l 2-5 -n 4 -- --forward-mode=io --nb-cores=3
# NIC disappears from 'ip link'

check.q: Why does a DPDK-bound NIC disappear from ip link?
check.a: It's unbound from the kernel driver and owned by the user-space poll-mode driver.
